bigPicture.subtitle: The Man in Chains Who Told You Where You Are Seated
paragraphs: Picture the room where this letter was written. Rome, somewhere around AD 60 to 62. A rented house, a permanent guard, and a manacle running from one man’s wrist to a soldier’s. Under Roman military custody the prisoner does not sit alone; the empire attaches itself to him physically, and every time he shifts his weight another man’s arm moves. That is the posture of the writer. And when he finally tells you about it, near the end, he uses a word that should be impossible in the same sentence as a chain: “for which I am an ambassador in chains” (6:20). Ambassador is πρεσβεύω (presbeúō, G4243), the verb for a senior envoy sent to represent a sovereign power. In the ancient world an ambassador was untouchable — you laid a hand on him and you had declared war on his king. This one is in irons. Chains is ἅλυσις (hálysis, G254), a fetter, a manacle. So here is a diplomat of heaven, bound by the government he was sent to. And the very first thing out of his mouth is not his case, not his health, not his appeal to Caesar. It is this: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (1:3). Blessed is εὐλογητός (eulogētós, G2128); blessing is εὐλογία (eulogía, G2129). Read the whole letter knowing this: the man describing your throne cannot stand up without permission.

Now, what kind of letter is it? The text in front of you reads “to the saints who are at Ephesus, and the faithful in Christ Jesus” (1:1) — and honesty requires saying that those two words, in Ephesus, are missing from the earliest and best copies we possess. The oldest surviving papyrus collection of Paul’s letters, copied around AD 200, carries no city name there at all, and neither do the original hands of the two great fourth-century codices; later scribes put Ephesus in. What those oldest copies leave behind is a sentence hanging in mid-air — to the saints who are, and faithful in Christ Jesus — with the words who are still holding the door open for a place that was never written down. And the letter behaves exactly like a letter with a blank in it. Romans ends with a roll-call of more than two dozen names. Colossians names Epaphras, Onesimus, Archippus, Nympha. Ephesians names exactly one human being besides Paul — Tychicus, the man carrying it: “whom I have sent to you for this very purpose, that you may know our state, and that he may comfort your hearts” (6:22). No local crisis is corrected. No opponent is answered. No sin is named with an address attached. And this from a man who spent three years in Ephesus, longer than anywhere else Luke records, and who knelt and prayed with the elders of that church at Miletus while they wept on his neck and walked him down to the ship (Acts 20:31, 36–38). The strongest reading of that evidence is that this was a circular — a letter meant to be read aloud in one town and then carried up the road to the next, all round the province of Asia, with the reader in each place supplying the name of his own city. Paul tells the Colossians to make sure they read the letter coming to them from Laodicea (Colossians 4:16); many think you are holding it. Which means the blank in verse 1 is not damage. It is an invitation. Your town goes in it. Your name goes in it.

The shape of the thing is the most symmetrical Paul ever built. Chapters 1 to 3 are one long declaration of what God has done. Chapters 4 to 6 are how you now walk. Go through the first half and notice who owns the verbs: God chose, predestined, freely gave, redeemed, forgave, made known, sealed, raised, seated, made alive, brought near, broke down, reconciled, built, filled. You are the object of nearly every one of them. The only thing you are actually told to do in the first three chapters is remember what you used to be: “Therefore remember that once you, the Gentiles in the flesh…” (2:11). Then the hinge turns: “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called” (4:1). Therefore. Everything after that word stands on everything before it. And walk — περιπατέω (peripatéō, G4043), to tread all around, to conduct your whole life — becomes the drumbeat of the back half: walk worthily (4:1), no longer walk as the rest of the Gentiles walk (4:17), “Walk in love” (5:2), “Walk as children of light” (5:8), “watch carefully how you walk” (5:15). And then, at the very end, you stop walking and you stand (6:11–14). Here is the law of this letter, and if you break it you have broken the book: nothing is commanded in chapters 4 to 6 that is not first given in chapters 1 to 3. You do not walk in order to get seated. You walk because you already are.

And do not let anyone hand you this book as a soothing devotional. Ephesus was the occult capital of the ancient world. The temple of Artemis there was one of the seven wonders; the city traded so heavily in written spells that “Ephesian letters” was a recognised term for magical formulas; and Luke records converts burning their books of magic in a public bonfire valued at fifty thousand pieces of silver (Acts 19:19). Paul is not writing calming thoughts to comfortable people. He is writing to men and women converted out of a power-cult, and he tells them there is a real hierarchy of unseen authority — ἀρχή (archḗ, G746), rule; ἐξουσία (exousía, G1849), authority; κοσμοκράτωρ (kosmokrátōr, G2888), world-ruler — and that Christ has already been seated “far above all rule, and authority, and power, and dominion, and every name that is named, not only in this age, but also in that which is to come” (1:21). Then there is the wall. In Herod’s temple a low stone barrier ran around the inner courts, carved with notices in Greek and Latin warning that any foreigner who passed it had only himself to blame for the death that followed; two of those stones have been dug out of the ground and can be seen today. Paul is wearing this chain because a mob accused him of taking a Gentile past that barrier — and the Gentile they named was Trophimus the Ephesian (Acts 21:29). Sit with that for a moment. A man imprisoned over a wall, writing to the province that man came from, to say: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of partition” (2:14). Middle wall is μεσότοιχον (mesótoichon, G3320); partition is φραγμός (phragmós, G5418), a fence, an enclosing barrier. He is in a cell for a wall, announcing that the wall is rubble.

Twice in this letter the prisoner stops and prays out loud, and what he asks for will reorganise your prayer life. Not release. Not health. Not a favourable verdict. Not even safety. He prays “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him; having the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (1:17–18), and later, on his knees, “that you may be strengthened with power through his Spirit in the inward man” (3:16). A man who cannot change his own circumstances, praying that free people would stop staring at theirs. That is Ephesians. It will take you up into a decision God made “before the foundation of the world” (1:4), walk you through a graveyard where dead men are made alive, tear down a wall between peoples who genuinely hated each other, seat you above every named power in the universe, and then hand you armour and tell you the fight is real: “For our wrestling is not against flesh and blood” (6:12). Wrestling is πάλη (pálē, G3823) — not archery, not siege warfare; hand-to-hand, close enough to feel breath. This letter will not let you have the comfort without the combat, or the combat without the throne.

bridge.intro: The Holy Spirit set Ephesians directly after Galatians because freedom produces two very different documents: the one written while it is being fought for, and the one written once it has been won.

points.title: From the Battlefield to the Reading of the Will
points.body: Galatians is a gospel under armed attack, and Paul writes like a man defending a wounded friend. He skips the thanksgiving entirely and opens with a wound: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). He pronounces a curse, then repeats it in case anyone thought he misspoke (1:8–9). He calls them “Foolish Galatians” (3:1). And in one white-hot line about the men pushing circumcision on his converts he writes, “I wish that those who disturb you would cut themselves off” (5:12) — if you are going to trust the knife, go all the way with it. Now open Ephesians. No opponent is named. No curse is pronounced. No crisis is being put out. The same doctrine, the same apostle, an entirely different room — because Galatians ends its great argument at a sentence it never gets time to unpack: “So you are no longer a bondservant, but a son; and if a son, then an heir of God through Christ” (Galatians 4:7). Ephesians is the reading of the will. Inheritance is κληρονομία (klēronomía, G2817), and that word-family runs through the first chapter like a solicitor’s voice. First the verb: “in whom also we were assigned an inheritance” (1:11) — κληρόω (klēróō, G2820), to allot, to assign a man his portion by lot. Then the noun, twice: the Spirit “who is a pledge of our inheritance” (1:14) — ἀῤῥαβών (arrhabṓn, G728), the down payment handed over in advance as legal security that the rest is coming — and “the riches of the glory of his inheritance in the saints” (1:18). Galatians shouts you are not a slave. Ephesians opens the estate papers and quietly shows you the size of what you inherited.

points.title: The Wall Peter Rebuilt and the Wall Christ Demolished
points.body: The most painful scene in Galatians happens at a dinner table. “But when Peter came to Antioch, I resisted him to his face, because he stood condemned. For before some people came from James, he ate with the Gentiles. But when they came, he drew back and separated himself, fearing those who were of the circumcision” (Galatians 2:11–12) — and it spread, until “even Barnabas was carried away with their hypocrisy” (2:13). That is a wall going back up, one chair at a time, over a meal. Galatians has to fight for the demolition. Ephesians surveys the site and describes the building that replaced it. Christ did not soften the hostility — He executed it: “having abolished in his flesh the hostility… that he might create in himself one new man of the two, making peace” (2:15), “and might reconcile them both in one body to God through the cross, having killed the hostility thereby” (2:16). Not Gentiles turned into Jews. Not Jews turned into Gentiles. One new man, a third thing that had never existed on the earth before. Galatians 3:28 tells you what is no longer true — “There is neither Jew nor Greek, there is neither slave nor free man, there is neither male nor female; for you are all one in Christ Jesus.” Ephesians 2 tells you what is true instead: “you are no longer strangers and foreigners, but you are fellow citizens with the saints, and of the household of God” (2:19). Fellow citizen is συμπολίτης (sympolítēs, G4847), a man from the same town as you — and it ends with the whole structure becoming “a habitation of God in the Spirit” (2:22), κατοικητήριον (katoikētḗrion, G2732), a dwelling-place. The rubble of the wall became the foundation of the temple.

points.title: From the Curse He Became to the Blessing He Poured
points.body: Galatians takes you to the darkest transaction in Scripture: “Christ redeemed us from the curse of the law, having become a curse for us. For it is written, ‘Cursed is everyone who hangs on a tree’” (Galatians 3:13). The verb there is ἐξαγοράζω (exagorázō, G1805) — to buy up out of the market, to purchase something and take it out of circulation forever. Ephesians opens with the other side of the same ledger: “in whom we have our redemption through his blood, the forgiveness of our trespasses, according to the riches of his grace” (1:7). Redemption here is ἀπολύτρωσις (apolýtrōsis, G629), the ransom paid in full, and riches is πλοῦτος (ploûtos, G4149), a word Paul cannot stop using in this letter. Same blood, two angles. Galatians tells you what your freedom cost Him. Ephesians tells you what it bought you. And notice which one had to come first: a man who has not stood at the tree and watched the curse land on Someone Else will always read Ephesians 1 as poetry. Read it as a receipt.

points.title: From “Walk by the Spirit” to “Walk Worthy”
points.body: Galatians closes its ethics with a walk and a harvest: “walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh” (5:16); “the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (5:22–23); “Bear one another’s burdens, and so fulfill the law of Christ” (6:2). Ephesians takes that same walk and marches it straight indoors — into your mouth (“Let no corrupt speech proceed out of your mouth”, 4:29), your temper before bedtime (“Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath”, 4:26), your hands and your wallet (“let him labor, producing with his hands something that is good, that he may have something to give to him who has need”, 4:28), your marriage (5:22–33), your children (6:1–4), and your job (6:5–9). Freedom in Galatians is a doctrine defended in public. Freedom in Ephesians is a doctrine walked out in a kitchen. And there is one more thread to catch. Galatians signs off with a scarred body: “I bear the marks of the Lord Jesus branded on my body” (6:17). Turn the page, and the scarred man is in a chain — and the chain has become a pulpit: “an ambassador in chains” (6:20). The freedom he bled for in Galatians, he now unfolds from a cell. Which is the only real proof that the freedom was never about circumstances in the first place.

coreTheme.title: In the Heavenly Places
paragraphs: One phrase holds this entire letter upright, and it occurs nowhere else in the Bible. ἐν τοῖς ἐπουρανίοις — en tois epouraníois — built on the adjective ἐπουράνιος (epouránios, G2032), which means simply above the sky. That adjective turns up all over the New Testament; this exact phrase does not. Five times in six chapters, and not one occurrence anywhere else in the Bible. Notice something about the Greek: there is no word for places in it at all. Paul writes in the heavenlies, and English translators supply the noun because our language will not tolerate a floating adjective. So do not picture a postcode with clouds. Picture the realm where actual authority sits — the unseen dimension that decides what happens in the seen one. And then watch Paul use that one phrase five times to nail the whole letter together.

Trace it, because this is the spine. First, that is where the blessings are: “who has blessed us with every spiritual blessing in the heavenly places in Christ” (1:3) — which means your account is not held anywhere thieves, governments, recessions, or a diagnosis can reach it. Second, that is where Christ is: God “raised him from the dead, and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places, far above all rule, and authority, and power, and dominion” (1:20–21), and then “He put all things in subjection under his feet, and gave him to be head over all things for the assembly” (1:22). Third — and this is the sentence that should stop your breath — that is where you are: “and raised us up with him, and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” (2:6). Fourth, that is the auditorium where the church is on display: “to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places” (3:10). Manifold is πολυποίκιλος (polypoíkilos, G4182) — much-variegated, many-coloured, the kind of word you would use of embroidery; God’s wisdom is a tapestry and the church is the piece hanging on the wall, and the powers are the gallery. Fifth, that is where the war is: “against the spiritual forces of wickedness in the heavenly places” (6:12). Now put the five side by side. The blessings, the Christ, the you, the exhibition, and the war are all at one address.

That address is not a novelty of Paul’s. It is where the whole Bible has been pointing. Psalm 110 opens with the LORD telling David’s Lord to sit at His right hand until His enemies are made His footstool — the single most quoted Old Testament verse in the New Testament — and Ephesians 1:20–22 is that psalm cashed in: seated, and everything under His feet. The letter Tychicus carried in the same bag, to Colossae, says the same thing from the other side: you were raised with Christ, so set your mind on what is above, where He is seated. Hebrews keeps circling one astonishing detail about our High Priest — He sat down. Every other priest in history stood, because the work was never finished. And to the church at Laodicea, one of the very towns on this letter’s delivery route, the risen Christ would later promise the overcomer a seat on His own throne (Revelation 3:21). The Bible’s storyline does not end with you rescued. It ends with you enthroned in the Rescuer.

So land it where you actually live. There are two ways to lose this letter, and most believers pick one of them. The first is to fight for a seat you already occupy — which is why accusation flattens you, why one bad week feels like a verdict, why you keep re-auditioning for a Father who already adopted you. The second is to enjoy the seat and deny the war — which is why so many sincere Christians are permanently ambushed and permanently surprised. Ephesians refuses both. You fight from the throne, not toward it. That is exactly why the command in chapter 6 is never advance and never conquer; the word lands four times in as many lines — “able to stand against the wiles of the devil” (6:11), “able to withstand in the evil day, and, having done all, to stand” (6:13), “Stand therefore” (6:14). Stand is ἵστημι (hístēmi, G2476). The ground was taken at the cross and the seat was assigned at the resurrection; your assignment is to still be standing on it when the smoke clears. So the next time accusation walks into the room, do not argue about your worth from the floor. Answer from the chair.

truths.intro: As we journey through these 6 chapters, the Holy Spirit wants to anchor these truths in your spirit:

items.title: Nothing Is Commanded in Chapters 4–6 That Is Not First Given in Chapters 1–3
items.body: The whole letter pivots on one word — therefore. “I therefore, the prisoner in the Lord, beg you to walk worthily of the calling with which you were called” (4:1). Worthily is ἀξίως (axíōs, G516), which means fittingly, appropriately, in a manner that matches; calling is κλῆσις (klēsis, G2821), an invitation already issued. Paul is not telling you to walk in order to become worthy of a calling; he is telling you to walk in a way that fits a calling you already have. A soldier does not put on the uniform in order to be enlisted. He wears it because he is. And Ephesians says it flatly, with no small print: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast” (2:8–9). Grace is χάρις (cháris, G5485), a gift given for the joy of the Giver, never a wage owed to a worker. Then comes the verse that puts your good works exactly where they belong: “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them” (2:10). Workmanship is ποίημα (poíēma, G4161) — a made thing, a product, something crafted by a maker. And read the last clause slowly: the works were prepared beforehand. You do not manufacture them under pressure to prove something. You walk into ground that was laid before you arrived. So watch your own heart as you read the back half of this letter. The moment chapters 4 to 6 start to feel like the price of your acceptance rather than the shape of it, you have turned the book upside down, and you will end up exhausted, religious, and secretly resentful. Read the commands with your seat under you.

items.title: Dead Men Do Not Improve — They Get Raised
items.body: Ephesians will not let you have grace until you have accepted the diagnosis. “You were made alive when you were dead in transgressions and sins” (2:1). Dead is νεκρός (nekrós, G3498) — not sick, not slipping, not underperforming, not a good person having a rough decade. Dead. And busy: “in which you once walked according to the course of this world, according to the prince of the power of the air, the spirit who now works in the children of disobedience” (2:2), and “were by nature children of wrath, even as the rest” (2:3). By nature. Not by accident, not by bad influence — by species. Then come the two words that hold up the New Testament: “But God, being rich in mercy, for his great love with which he loved us” (2:4). And then three verbs, and in the Greek every one of them is welded to the preposition with: “made us alive together with Christ” — συζωοποιέω (syzōopoiéō, G4806); “raised us up with him” — συνεγείρω (synegeírō, G4891); “and made us to sit with him in the heavenly places in Christ Jesus” — συγκαθίζω (synkathízō, G4776), to give a seat in company with (2:5–6). You were not handed a second chance; a second chance is useless to a corpse. You were handed a second life, and it is His — whatever happened to Jesus on resurrection morning happened to you in Him. And mind the tense: made us to sit. Past. Finished. Your seat is not a retirement package that matures when you die. It is your current address. Which means the question for this week is not whether you can climb up there. It is whether you will live like a man who is already there.

items.title: The Wall Came Down So the War Could Be Won
items.body: The two ends of this letter are one truth, and most people read them as if they were unrelated. At the front: “For he is our peace, who made both one, and broke down the middle wall of partition, having abolished in his flesh the hostility” (2:14–15). Notice where the hatred died — in his flesh, “through the cross, having killed the hostility thereby” (2:16). God did not negotiate a truce between peoples who despised each other; He executed the hostility in the body of His Son. And then chapter 3 tells you why He went to that length: “to the intent that now through the assembly the manifold wisdom of God might be made known to the principalities and the powers in the heavenly places” (3:10). Assembly is ἐκκλησία (ekklēsía, G1577). A church where former enemies eat together is not a nice social outcome. It is evidence, submitted before an unseen court, that God’s wisdom outmanoeuvred every power in the universe. Now you know why Paul says “our wrestling is not against flesh and blood” (6:12). The exhibit is under attack. That is why congregations fracture along the fault lines of race, class, tribe, tongue and family; why the argument in the church car park carries a heat wildly out of proportion to its subject. Something is trying to smash the display case. So God issues equipment: “Put on the whole armor of God” (6:11) — πανοπλία (panoplía, G3833), the full panoply, everything, not a selection you are free to shop from — against “the wiles of the devil”, μεθοδεία (methodeía, G3180), which carries the sense of scheming, a method, a worked-out strategy against you. And here is the detail that changes the whole picture: this is not first of all the kit of the Roman guard chained to Paul’s wrist, though he had one in front of him day and night. It is God’s own armour. Isaiah 59:17 describes the LORD Himself putting on righteousness as a breastplate and a helmet of salvation, arming Himself to go and rescue a world that could not save itself. Ephesians 6 is God taking off His armour and strapping it onto you.

preparation.intro: Before we step into Chapter 1, prepare your spirit with these reflections:

items.title: The Seat You Have Never Sat In
items.body: Do this before you read a line of chapter 1, and do it with a pen. Read 1:3–14 out loud without stopping. In the Greek it is one single unbroken sentence — one of the longest in the New Testament — because Paul will not let you interrupt him. Now go back through it and underline every verb where God is the one acting: blessed, chose, predestined, freely gave, made known, purposed — and then the last two, where you are the grammatical subject but He is still the one doing it, we were assigned an inheritance and you were sealed. Chose is ἐκλέγομαι (eklégomai, G1586), to select; predestined is προορίζω (proorízō, G4309), to mark out the boundary in advance — and what He marked you out for is υἱοθεσία (huiothesía, G5206), adoption, the placing of a person into the full standing of a son; sealed is σφραγίζω (sphragízō, G4972), to stamp with a signet for security and ownership. Then underline every verb where you are the one acting. Count the two lists. Now answer honestly, out loud, alone: which list have I been living out of? Then get specific and name the room where you still behave like a beggar at the gate instead of a son at the table — the prayer you cannot start without first submitting your résumé of good behaviour; the sin you have re-confessed eleven times because you cannot believe it was forgiven the first; the one person whose approval quietly functions as your real verdict. Write that room down somewhere only you will see it. Ephesians is coming for it.

items.title: The Wall in Your Own House
items.body: Two questions, and do not flinch at either. First: who is the person, family, tribe, tongue, denomination, or class you have quietly filed under not really my people? Be concrete — a name, not a category. Because Christ did not merely disapprove of that wall; He killed the hostility in His own flesh (2:15–16), and if that hostility is still breathing inside you, then you are personally maintaining a structure God demolished at the cost of His Son’s body. Say the name out loud, then plan one concrete act of nearness this week: a meal, a phone call, an apology, a seat at your table. Second, prepare yourself for 5:22–6:9 before you arrive there, because the household code has been abused in both directions for two thousand years — softened into meaninglessness, or sharpened into a weapon. Settle two facts now. Every clause of it sits underneath 5:21, “subjecting yourselves to one another in the fear of Christ” — ὑποτάσσω (hypotássō, G5293) — and in the oldest manuscripts verse 22 has no verb of its own at all; it reaches back and borrows the verb from verse 21. And Paul gives the husband roughly three times more instruction than the wife, and every line of it is about dying: “Husbands, love your wives, even as Christ also loved the assembly, and gave himself up for it” (5:25). So ask yourself the question now, while there is still time to repent of the answer: whose submission have I been quietly requiring, while skipping the verses addressed to me about laying my life down?

prayerOfActivation: Father of glory, I open this letter from a chained man, and I ask You for the one thing he asked for. Not easier circumstances — sight. Give me a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of You. Enlighten the eyes of my heart, that I may know the hope of Your calling, the riches of the glory of Your inheritance in the saints, and the exceeding greatness of Your power toward me because I believe. Lord, I confess I have read about a throne I have never sat on. Before You show me anything else, show me what I was: dead in transgressions and sins, walking in step with the course of this world, by nature a child of wrath, with nothing in my hands and no case to make. And then let those two words land on me like sunrise — but God. But God, being rich in mercy, for Your great love with which You loved me, made me alive together with Christ, raised me up with Him, and made me to sit with Him in the heavenly places. I receive that as fact and not feeling. I stop auditioning for a Father who has already adopted me. By grace I have been saved through faith, and that not of myself; it is Your gift, not of works, so that I cannot boast — and I refuse to rebuild with my performance what You demolished with Your blood. Jesus, You are my peace. Wherever there is still a wall standing in me — against a people, a family, a tribe, a church, a person whose name I know — tear it down. You killed that hostility in Your own flesh; do not let me keep it alive in mine. Make me a fellow citizen who acts like one. Holy Spirit, You sealed me for the day of redemption; I will not grieve You. Strengthen me with power in the inward man. Let Christ dwell in my heart through faith. Root me and ground me in love until I comprehend the width and length and height and depth, and know the love of Christ which surpasses knowledge, and am filled with all the fullness of God. Then teach me to walk — worthily of the calling with which I was called; in lowliness and patience, bearing with people I find hard; in truth spoken with love; with a mouth that builds instead of tearing down; with hands that work so I have something to give; forgiving others exactly as You in Christ forgave me. Make me an imitator of You, walking in love, walking as a child of light, watching carefully how I walk, redeeming the time because the days are evil, filled with Your Spirit, subjecting myself to others in the fear of Christ. And when the fight comes — and it is coming — let me be strong in You and in the strength of Your might. I put on the whole armour of God today, all of it, not the pieces I prefer. Buckle truth around me. Cover my heart with righteousness. Fit my feet with the Good News of peace. Put the shield of faith in my hand to quench every fiery dart, the helmet of salvation on my head, and the sword of the Spirit, which is Your word, in my mouth. My wrestling is not against flesh and blood, so let me stop fighting people and start standing against powers. Having done all — let me stand. And Lord, do in me exceedingly abundantly above all that I ask or think, according to the power that works in me. To You be the glory in the assembly and in Christ Jesus, to all generations, forever and ever. In the mighty name of Jesus, Amen!
